title: SONA CLI
markdown:
# SONA CLI

Use the CLI to read SONA performance reports and follow target lifecycle events from a terminal. It uses your account's MFA and organization permissions. It does not place trades, regenerate reports, or send notifications.

- [Install and sign in](getting-started.md)
- [Commands](commands.md)
- [JSON and CSV exports](exports.md)
- [Understand the numbers](understanding-results.md)
- [Watch live targets](live-watch.md)
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)
- [API and contributor reference](development.md)
- [Verification and release gates](verification.md)
- [Postman collection and environment templates](postman/README.md)
- [Phased release acceptance](release-acceptance.md)

Version: 0.1.0. Supported runtime: Node.js 22 or newer. Supported credential-storage platforms: macOS and Linux with private POSIX file permissions. Windows credential persistence is not certified.

Package publication and backend deployment are separate release steps; source availability alone does not mean that a live environment supports watch mode. All CLI data requests use the separately authorized `/api/cli` interfaces; watch mode requires the backend additions described in the contributor guide. All examples use placeholders or synthetic data.

## Quick reference

Set `SONA_BASE_URL` to your trusted dashboard service root and `SONA_API_KEY` to its Firebase project's public web API key, download the approved archive from **CLI & Documentation** in your dashboard, verify its checksum, then install and sign in:

```sh
npm install --global ./harper-vance-sona-cli-0.1.0.tgz
sona login
sona daily --date 2026-10-01
sona monthly --month 2026-10 --details
sona watch
```

Choose a date available within your organization's history window. The examples above are illustrative historical selectors, not promises of accessible reports for those dates. `sona --help` and `sona --version` do not require configuration or sign-in.

title: Installation and authentication
markdown:
# Installation and authentication

## Prerequisites

Use Node.js 22+ on macOS or Linux, an existing account with an enrolled authenticator, and an organization licensed for the features you request. Enroll or recover MFA through the dashboard’s security settings. Contact support if you cannot access your authenticator. The CLI does not enroll factors, create accounts, change passwords, or bypass MFA. When multiple authenticators are enrolled it uses the first TOTP enrollment returned by Identity Platform.

## Install

Open **CLI & Documentation** in your dashboard. Choose your organization and download the supported release. CLI access is included with Desk Intelligence and Firm Wide Enterprise; Entity Core is excluded. Custom licenses require an explicit grant. Existing organizations need a newly issued entitlement containing `cli.access`; absent grants deny access until provisioned. Active membership and existing report/history permissions still apply.

Use Node.js 22+ on macOS or Linux. Verify the downloaded file against the SHA-256 checksum displayed in the dashboard:

```sh
shasum -a 256 harper-vance-sona-cli-0.1.0.tgz
npm install -g ./harper-vance-sona-cli-0.1.0.tgz
sona --version
sona --help
```

Download a newer approved version from the dashboard and install its archive the same way to update. Keep the prior verified archive to recover a compatible earlier version; installing an old executable does not restore expired access or an incompatible server interface. To remove the package:

```sh
sona logout
npm uninstall -g @harper-vance/sona-cli
```

Contributors may install from `cli/` in the source checkout. The package has no external runtime dependencies. Copying an archive never grants product access; the service checks eligibility on every CLI request.

## Configuration

There is deliberately no production URL default. Obtain the correct service root and Firebase public web API key from your administrator. The base URL is the dashboard/API service origin, or the deployed function URL including its function path, before `/api/cli/product`. Do not append `/api` to it.

```sh
export SONA_BASE_URL='https://your-dashboard.example'
export SONA_API_KEY='your-project-public-web-api-key'
export SONA_ORGANIZATION='your-organization-id'
sona login
```

The API key identifies the Firebase project; it does not authorize product access. The organization option is optional and otherwise uses the account's default organization.

Configuration precedence is command-line option, environment, then optional JSON configuration file. Pass `--config /absolute/path/config.json` or set `SONA_CONFIG`. Supported JSON properties are `baseUrl`, `apiKey`, and `organization`. Equivalent flags are `--base-url`, `--api-key`, and `--organization`. URLs must use HTTPS, except loopback HTTP for isolated local testing. Embedded URL credentials, query strings, fragments, and redirects are rejected.

## Sign in

`sona login` privately prompts for your email, password, and six-digit authenticator code. Nothing typed into these prompts is echoed, and passwords/codes are not accepted as arguments or environment variables. A real terminal is required. CAPTCHA-enforced or federated-only accounts may require an additional future authentication integration; the current login supports Identity Platform email/password plus enrolled TOTP.

After MFA, the CLI verifies the token against `/api/cli/access` before saving the session. It uses [Identity Platform password sign-in](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/reference/rest/v1/accounts/signInWithPassword), [TOTP challenge completion](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/reference/rest/v2/accounts.mfaSignIn/finalize), and [Firebase refresh tokens](https://firebase.google.com/docs/reference/rest/auth#section-refresh-token). A first-factor-only token is rejected. Product access is always checked by the service.

## Local credentials and sign-out

The default session directory is `~/.sona-cli` with mode `0700`; session files use `0600`. `SONA_STATE_DIR` can select a separate private directory. Sessions are bound to the exact service URL and API key. Shared directories, unsafe permissions, symbolic-link files, and files owned by someone else are rejected.

**Session files contain unencrypted ID/refresh tokens protected by operating-system ownership and file permissions.** They are not stored in the system keychain. Protect the computer account and disk, and do not copy these files into repositories, shared folders, backups shared with others, or support messages. This storage approach is supported on macOS/Linux, not certified on Windows. The password and authenticator code are never persisted.

Tokens renew before expiration using the configured project's secure-token endpoint. A rejected refresh clears the local session; run `sona login` again. Sign out locally with:

```sh
sona logout
```

This removes the selected service's local credentials. It does not revoke sessions on other computers; use dashboard account controls for that.

## First report

```sh
sona daily --date 2026-10-01 --format json
```

Choose an accessible completed session. Missing history is different from missing permission. See [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md). No ordinary CLI operation needs a service-account key or administrative database credentials.

title: Command reference
markdown:
# Command reference

Every data command requires a configured service and sign-in. All dates use New York reporting time, independent of the terminal's local timezone. Invalid/future selectors fail before an API read. The service remains authoritative for reporting calendars, coverage, and history access.

| Command | Selection and defaults | Access | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `daily` | Required `--date` or `--dates`; up to 60 unique comma-separated dates | Daily reports | `sona daily --date 2026-10-01 --details` |
| `weekly` | Required `--year` and `--week`, using ISO week year | Weekly reports | `sona weekly --year 2020 --week 53 --format json` |
| `monthly` | Required `--month YYYY-MM` | History | `sona monthly --month 2026-10 --details` |
| `rolling` | `--sessions 10`, `20`, or `40`; defaults to 20. Optional `--end-date` | History | `sona rolling --sessions 40 --end-date 2026-10-01` |
| `targets` | Optional `--date`; defaults to current New York date; current date only | Live targets | `sona targets --format json` |
| `history` | Required `--dates`; up to 60 unique comma-separated dates | History | `sona history --dates 2026-10-01 --format csv` |
| `context` | Optional `--date`; defaults to current New York date; current date only | Daily reports | `sona context --format json` |
| `watch` | Optional current `--date`, optional `--cursor` for same-day recovery | Live targets | `sona watch --format json` |

Dates outside your history window may be syntactically valid but denied by the service. For ISO weeks, the ISO year can differ from the calendar year near January 1. Week 53 is accepted only when that ISO year has 53 weeks. Historical targets are obtained through daily/monthly rows, not by sending historical dates to the live endpoint.

## Common options

- `--format table|json|csv`: default `table`. JSON watch output is newline-delimited records, not a single JSON document.
- `--details`: include available direction, time-of-day, timing, pullback, streak, miss, and comparison sections. It never creates missing legacy fields.
- `--rows summary|targets|days|candles`: select tabular/CSV row granularity. JSON includes the normalized document; selecting target rows adds target detail when the report API supports it.
- `--base-url`, `--api-key`, `--organization`, `--config`: see [configuration](getting-started.md).
- `--help`, `--version`: offline commands. Unknown/duplicate options and positional credential values are rejected.

| Command | Accepted row selectors |
|---|---|
| daily | summary (daily rows), days, targets |
| weekly | summary |
| monthly | summary, days, targets |
| rolling | summary, days |
| targets | summary (target rows), targets |
| history | summary (candle rows), candles |
| context | summary |
| watch | summary; uses its separate event format |

Weekly/rolling report APIs do not return individual target rows. Use permitted daily/monthly target listings for those details. Empty available row lists produce empty CSV or a terminal message; wholly unavailable daily/weekly reports exit with status 5.

## Additional examples

```sh
sona daily --dates 2026-10-01,2026-10-02 --rows targets --format csv
sona monthly --month 2026-10 --rows days --format csv
sona monthly --month 2026-10 --rows targets --format json
sona targets --organization your-organization-id
sona watch --format csv
```

Examples use illustrative dates; replace them with dates licensed for your organization. Snapshot commands make a finite read. Watch keeps making bounded event reads until interrupted, closed-session drain completes, date changes, access is lost, or reconnect attempts are exhausted. See [live watch](live-watch.md) and [exports/exit statuses](exports.md).

title: Understanding SONA results
markdown:
# Understanding SONA results

Targets reached are not trades won or account profits. A target is a monitored price level. Whether a real trade makes money also depends on entry, exit, sizing, costs, and risk decisions, which these reports do not measure.

| Measure | What it means |
|---|---|
| Created / hits / missed | Recorded targets and completed-session outcomes. An open live target is not yet a completed-session miss. |
| Accuracy | Total hits divided by total targets, as a percentage. No targets means unavailable accuracy, not 0%. |
| Median time | Typical time among measured hits, measured using the existing close-to-close reporting rules. |
| Average time | Mean among measured hits; slow outliers affect it more than the median. |
| Pullback/retraction | Price movement away from the target before the reversal that reached it, measured in points on hits. |
| Percentiles | How measurements are distributed. The middle 50% lies between the 25th and 75th percentiles. |
| Closest miss | How close a missed target came during the supported evaluation window; it is unavailable when measurement history is insufficient. |
| Sample count | Number of usable observations for that metric; it can be smaller than total hits. |

For example, a 1/1 day and a 1/9 day combine to **2/10 = 20%**. Averaging their daily percentages would give about 55.6%, which describes a different calculation. Headline weekly accuracy uses pooled counts. Monthly and recent-session totals use the existing server calculations. Medians are never recomputed by averaging daily medians.

## Periods and comparisons

New York reporting sessions, weekends, holidays and early closes come from existing server calendar rules. Today's daily report is not treated as a completed report until the existing reporting workflow produces it. The current calendar month remains in progress. Rolling reports select 10, 20, or 40 completed sessions, with server-managed warm-up for trend calculations.

Weekly `weekStats` describes the chosen week. Weekly rolling-context groups can cover a different recent window; prior-period context excludes the selected week. Detail labels retain these separate blocks. Monthly comparisons use the prior calendar month when complete and licensed. Partial-month volume comparisons use targets/hits per included session as provided by the API. Best/worst days should be read with target counts: a perfect one-target day has a smaller sample than a perfect ten-target day.

## Data quality

- **Zero targets:** an available session with no targets. It counts as a session, with unavailable accuracy.
- **Missing / blocked / invalid:** records unavailable or withheld; these are not zero-activity sessions.
- **Closed:** calendar says no session. Not a losing day.
- **Pending / in progress:** the period is not finished. Do not treat it as final.
- **Legacy:** an earlier saved report version. Optional fields or compatible comparisons may be absent.
- **Unavailable measurements:** lack a usable timing, pullback, or distance observation. Do not replace them with zero.

Calendar-context comparison accuracy is stored as a fraction from 0 to 1 (for example, 0.9 means 90%); report headline accuracy remains a percent. Weekly saved best/worst labels may lack per-day sample counts in older reports; treat absent counts as unavailable rather than inventing them.

Coverage checks saved-record consistency; it does not by itself prove underlying candle history is complete. A replay gap in live watching is a separate event-delivery limitation and does not rewrite saved report outcomes.

Authoritative detail: [stats definitions](../stats.md), [time to resolution](../time-to-resolution.md), [retraction](../retraction.md), and [calendar context](../day-context.md). The CLI reuses these definitions and excludes internal entry-price/entry-heat diagnostics.

title: Live target watching
markdown:
# Live target watching

Run `sona watch` to follow target lifecycle changes. This requires the new backend event capture and event-read endpoint; installing the CLI alone does not deploy them. `sona targets` is a finite snapshot and cannot establish a complete lifecycle history.

## What you see

Watch starts with an active-target snapshot and then shows `created`, `updated`, `hit`, and `removed` events. Events remain in terminal output even when a target leaves the active list. Removal means a record was removed; it does not prove that its target hit. Hit is a separately confirmed source update.

A synthetic session might show a creation at 10:01, a hit at 10:03, then no active row. Both observed events remain above the next active snapshot. A target created and removed between two ordinary snapshot reads can still be recovered from the durable event journal. Events already captured before watch starts are not automatically presented as new history; the first read starts at the journal's current position with the current active snapshot.

The event log is retained in terminal output for the running process. It is not a durable local event database, and your terminal's scrollback settings can limit what you retain. Redirect NDJSON or CSV output to a file if you need an explicit archive:

```sh
sona watch --format json > session.ndjson
```

Treat exported market data according to your organization's access/license rules. No credentials appear in exports.

## Connection and replay behavior

Each authenticated event read waits at most **8 seconds**, then returns up to 100 events and a fresh source snapshot. Sessions above 250 source targets fail explicitly rather than silently dropping targets. The CLI immediately continues from its acknowledged cursor. This is bounded long polling of durable event history, not polling active targets and guessing events. Every new read checks MFA and organization permissions, and the backend rechecks token revocation/expiry and access after an idle wait before releasing data.

The public journal retains at most **1,000 lifecycle events per session**, additionally aged to 48 hours during append. Requests are **current New York date only**, so public recovery is limited by that date boundary as well as event count. Session cleanup runs daily and removes journal dates at least 48 hours old; it does not delete target/report sources. The backend permits two concurrent waits per user **per server instance**, plus existing request rate limits. It does not claim a distributed global connection quota.

On transient failure the HTTP reader makes up to three attempts. Watch can then make up to two reconnect attempts with finite backoff; an uninterrupted outage has at most nine HTTP attempts before failure. Access/input/session failures stop rather than repeatedly retrying credentials. Diagnostics identify connecting, live, reconnecting, failed, or stopped states. An expired replay position or reset journal produces an explicit gap record plus a fresh snapshot; the CLI never claims missing events were recovered.

Capture is asynchronous using retryable database-change events. **60 seconds after a committed backend change is an operational capture-lag budget, not a proven production latency guarantee.** The capture function logs measured lag and warns above budget. Platform outages, exhausted provider retries, or events before capture deployment cannot be reconstructed from active snapshots alone. Operators must monitor failed invocations and lag before relying on live completeness. Provider event retries do not resend Discord/email notifications. The journal sequence orders capture, which can differ from source timestamp order; active state is taken from fresh source snapshots to avoid regression.

## Ending a session

Ctrl+C cancels reads and releases server listeners. Session close is determined by the existing calendar, including early closes; watch allows a 60-second post-close drain before stopping. It also stops at New York date rollover instead of silently mixing sessions. A late provider capture after the drain is outside that run's observed history; a same-day reconnect can retrieve captured events with a known server cursor. The CLI currently retains cursors only in memory, so durable resume across process restarts is not promised.

For advanced clients, `--cursor` accepts the server-issued `YYYY-MM-DD:epoch:sequence` position for the same current date. Never fabricate a cursor to claim complete recovery. If sign-in expires, refresh is attempted between reads; revoked or denied access stops the watch. See [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

title: Output and exports
markdown:
# Output and exports

## Terminal

Default output is one readable record per line, with labeled fields. `--details` also prints structured detail sections. Common summary fields are `created`, `hits`, `missed`, `accuracy` (percent), `medianTime` (minutes or the saved human-readable minutes label), and `medianPullback` (points or the saved points label). Missing measurements display as `Unavailable`. Coverage and selected-period boundaries are included where supplied by the API.

## JSON

A finite report returns one JSON document with `kind`, `timezone`, and applicable `summary`, `period`, `coverage`, `days`, `targets`, or `details` properties. Daily results preserve each requested date and its `included`, `zero_targets`, `missing`, or `blocked` status. History groups projected candles by date; context provides event tags and comparison groups.

Projection excludes administrative/unknown fields and internal `entryPrice`/`entryHeatPoints`, including nested values. This is a documented public CLI projection rather than an unrestricted database dump. Numbers retain their source meaning; missing numeric observations stay null or absent. Existing daily/weekly formatted timing/pullback strings retain their units rather than being reinterpreted.

```sh
sona monthly --month 2026-10 --details --format json > month.json
```

Warnings and errors go to standard error. They never prefix JSON on standard output. A successful incomplete report can still return data with status 0 plus a coverage warning; inspect `coverage` and per-day statuses for analysis.

## CSV

`--rows` selects summary, daily, target, or candle rows as supported in the command table. Fields form the union of keys in the selected rows. Nested coverage/comparison/detail objects remain JSON-encoded cells, not silently flattened or discarded. Quotes are doubled and all cells are quoted. Missing values produce empty cells; zero remains zero. Text beginning with spreadsheet formula markers is prefixed with an apostrophe; numeric negative values remain numeric text without that prefix. Control characters in source strings are replaced with spaces.

```sh
sona daily --date 2026-10-01 --rows targets --format csv > targets.csv
sona history --dates 2026-10-01 --format csv > candles.csv
```

CSV/terminal row exports do not include every nested detail block; use JSON with `--details` when you need the complete projected breakdown. Row modes not supported by a command fail with status 2.

## Live output contract

Watch supports all three formats. JSON is NDJSON (one JSON object per line); CSV has one fixed header followed by records. Fields are `kind`, optional `id`, `date`, optional `sequence`, optional `sourceTime`, and `payload`:

- `snapshot`: current active-target array. This is distinct from the append-only observed event history.
- `created`, `updated`, `hit`, `removed`: target lifecycle events with a stable public event ID; payload includes the target ID and permitted target fields.
- `gap`: why some intervening event history could not be recovered.
- `session_closed` or `session_changed`: terminal session boundaries.

Source timestamps identify the committed source change, while sequence numbers order journal capture/delivery. Trigger delivery can arrive out of source-time order; current state uses fresh authoritative snapshots instead of applying late events as state mutations. JSON/CSV payloads are safe projections. Watch diagnostics go to standard error. The resume cursor is a server batch position; the CLI keeps it in memory for reconnects. Current output does not persist it to disk or expose a durable checkpoint file.

## Exit statuses

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Successful read, graceful watch/session end, or user cancellation; partial report warnings may still exist |
| 2 | Invalid command, option, period, or configuration |
| 3 | Sign-in/session/MFA/storage problem or missing interactive terminal |
| 4 | Access denied, including feature/history limits |
| 5 | Requested report unavailable |
| 6 | Service, response-format, timeout, network, or exhausted retry failure |

A failed request prints no report JSON/CSV. A long-running watch may have already emitted valid earlier records before a later failure; check its exit status and retain its preceding event records.

title: Troubleshooting
markdown:
# Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Safe next action | Escalate when |
|---|---|---|
| Invalid command/date/configuration (2) | Run `sona --help`; check strict dates, ISO week-year, row modes and service root. | A documented, supported input is rejected. |
| Sign-in/MFA/session error (3) | Check public Firebase key/service pairing; enroll TOTP in the dashboard; sign in again. Use a real terminal. | Enrollment or account recovery fails in the dashboard. |
| Unsafe session file (3) | Use an owner-only directory and file; do not bypass the ownership/symlink check. Remove only your selected local session if appropriate. | Managed-machine storage policies prevent private local files. |
| Access denied (4) | Check organization selection, feature license, account status, and requested history window. | Your administrator confirms the requested access should exist. |
| Report unavailable (5) | Try an accessible completed session; distinguish missing/blocked reports from zero-target days. | A report expected after scheduled generation remains missing. |
| Partial month or coverage warning (0) | Read `coverage` and per-day status; keep unavailable values separate from zero. | Completed expected sessions remain invalid/missing. |
| Service/network/timeout error (6) | Check connectivity and trusted base URL. Retry after the bounded command exits. | The service stays unavailable or health checks fail. |
| Rate limit or exhausted retries (6) | Reduce concurrent commands/watches and honor the service's retry guidance. | Expected licensed usage is consistently throttled. |
| Watch endpoint unavailable (5/6) | Confirm `targetEventCapture`, `targetEventCleanup`, and updated API are deployed. | Deployment claims completion but the endpoint is absent. |
| Watch reconnecting or stale | Retain output; allow its bounded recovery attempts. | Recovery fails or source changes persist without captured events. |
| Replay gap | Keep the gap record; treat refreshed active state separately from missing history. | Gaps recur within the documented supported window. |
| Export appears empty | Check requested row mode and whether data is available; inspect exit status and standard error. | Valid source rows are absent from a supported export. |
| Login blocked by CAPTCHA/federation | Use supported dashboard sign-in to confirm account status; do not disable account safeguards. | CLI REST sign-in requires an account flow not supported by this version. |

For support, provide CLI version, command name without credentials, requested date/period, sanitized service host, exit status, and a sanitized error/gap description. Administrators can correlate server-side request IDs from service logs. Do not share passwords, authenticator codes, token files, bearer headers, raw credential payloads, personal information, or unrestricted database exports.

Live capture operators should check `targetEvents.capture` lag warnings, failed/retried capture invocations, and event-read failures. An idle session alone does not prove capture health. Capture failures must be investigated against the committed source event; do not replay report or notification actions as a repair.

See [support/access recovery](../runbooks/support-and-access-recovery.md), [authentication](getting-started.md), [live watch](live-watch.md), and [exports/exit statuses](exports.md).

title: API and contributor reference
markdown:
# API and contributor reference

## Source boundaries

The standalone package is `cli/`, with executable `cli/bin/sona.js`. Runtime dependencies are Node built-ins. `config` validates arguments/selectors, `auth` adapts Identity Platform REST, `session` owns private files, `transport` owns finite reads, `output` projects public fields/formats, `watch` consumes durable batches, and `main` orchestrates commands. Modules do not run commands on import.

The backend retains routes → controllers → services. `functions/features/targetEvents/eventModel.js` owns public event projection, idempotent append and replay; `eventService.js` owns bounded subscriptions/revalidation; `eventController.js` maps HTTP; `eventCapture.js` defines retryable capture and retention functions. Existing report calculation helpers remain authoritative.

## API contract

All service reads return the existing `{success,data,meta,error}` envelope. Product routes require a Firebase Bearer ID token with authenticator TOTP MFA and organization entitlements. Optional `X-Organization-ID` selects the organization. Requests use `X-Request-ID`. The base URL is configurable; production requires HTTPS and redirects are rejected.

| CLI | Method and relative endpoint | Query | Required feature |
|---|---|---|---|
| daily | GET `/api/cli/product/daily` | `dates` comma-separated, 1–60 dates | dashboard.dailyReports |
| weekly | GET `/api/cli/product/weekly` | `year`, `week` (ISO) | dashboard.weeklyReports |
| monthly | GET `/api/cli/product/monthly` | `month` YYYY-MM | dashboard.history |
| rolling | GET `/api/cli/product/rolling` | `sessions` 10/20/40, optional `endDate` | dashboard.history |
| targets | GET `/api/cli/product/targets` | current `date` | dashboard.liveTargets |
| history | GET `/api/cli/product/history` | `dates` comma-separated, 1–60 dates | dashboard.history |
| context | GET `/api/cli/product/day-context` | current `date` | dashboard.dailyReports |
| watch (new backend) | GET `/api/cli/product/target-events` | current `date`, optional opaque `cursor` | dashboard.liveTargets |
| login verification | GET `/api/cli/access` | none | authenticated account |

Existing route source: `functions/features/productData/product_data_routes.js`; schemas: `product_data_schemas.js`; service: `product_data_service.js`; mount: `functions/server/index.js`. Raw `dates` is also bounded to 659 characters by the existing API. Daily response is date/data pairs; absent data and source-validation blocks remain explicit. Weekly can return null. Monthly returns summary, coverage, days/targets, distributions and optional prior comparison; rolling returns compact completed-session results. History returns date/candles pairs; context returns eventTags/buckets.

Native login uses the official [password](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/reference/rest/v1/accounts/signInWithPassword) and [MFA finalize](https://docs.cloud.google.com/identity-platform/docs/reference/rest/v2/accounts.mfaSignIn/finalize) interfaces, followed by server token verification. Refresh uses the [secure-token REST API](https://firebase.google.com/docs/reference/rest/auth#section-refresh-token). This native REST adapter deliberately owns renewal instead of introducing browser Firebase SDK persistence into a Node terminal. It stores refresh credentials in protected runtime session files rather than source `.env` files; these are explicit adaptations of the web/mobile-oriented SDK/storage standards. Passwords/codes remain transient and token claims are used only for refresh scheduling; the server verifies authorization.

## Event contract and consistency

`targetEventCapture` observes every committed write at `targets/nq/5m/{month}/{day}/{targetId}`, including writes from existing handlers, context writers, maintenance tools, and record deletion. It captures provider before/after snapshots and a SHA-256 provider event ID. Public-field-identical changes are omitted. Capture is retryable and idempotent using provider identities retained in a 48-hour receipt index. The event journal is server-only under `targetEventJournal/{date}`; existing deny-by-default database rules remain restrictive.

Target IDs are session-scoped SHA-256 aliases of source record keys; the public feed does not expose private database paths or keys. Each session journal has an epoch and transaction-allocated sequence. Event fields: `id`, `targetId`, `type` (`created|updated|hit|removed`), `sourceTime`, `target` public projection, `sequence`, `capturedAt`. Transactions bound replay to the latest 1,000 events and prune events older than 48 hours on append. Deduplication receipts outlive count-based event eviction. Capture does not rerun source writes or notifications. Failed captures remain provider retry work; alert on failed/exhausted invocations and lag. Provider retry delivery is not an unlimited historical recovery guarantee.

A batch returns `date`, `cursor`, `events`, `gap`, `targets`, `closed`, `limits`, and `asOf`. First reads acknowledge the captured journal position, then obtain current source state. Any source mutations during that handoff still produce later journal events; reads resume from the captured position. Current source state can be ahead of capture. Late/out-of-order capture remains visible in the event log; current active state is always refreshed from source, never inferred by applying capture-ordered events blindly.

Positions have the shape `date:epoch:sequence`. Gap reasons are `capture_reset`, `replay_expired`, or `session_changed`. A gap returns the bounded retained events plus fresh current state, without claiming complete reconstruction. A pending epoch means no event has yet been captured for that session. The response is a schema introduced with CLI/backend version 0.1.0; preserve field meaning within that version and document incompatible cursor/schema changes before release. A reset epoch invalidates old positions.

Long polls wait up to 8 seconds inside the API's existing 120-second function timeout; CLI requests have 10-second deadlines through body reading. The service rechecks revocation and organization access after waiting, before releasing target data. Disconnection cancels the listener, and an in-memory cap allows two waits per UID per API instance, alongside the existing read rate limiter. This is not a distributed global quota. Slow/disconnected clients do not accumulate unbounded server buffers: each response contains at most 100 journal events and 250 source targets (larger source states fail explicitly), and aged-out positions become explicit gaps. The CLI bounds response bodies to 8 MiB and suppresses duplicates using a recent-ID set. NDJSON/CSV consumers should also deduplicate by event ID when combining archives.

## Testing and adding commands

Use Node 22 and the repository's existing backend Jest setup; the dependency-free CLI uses Node's built-in test runner rather than installing a second test package:

```sh
npm --prefix cli test
npm --prefix functions test -- --runInBand --watchman=false
npm --prefix functions run lint
npm ci --prefix tools/postman --ignore-scripts
npm --prefix functions run test:e2e:cli
```

Add selector validation and a route mapping in `config`, a public projection/row contract in `output`, command help in the shared messages resource, and focused fixtures/tests. Put runtime labels in `cli/src/messages.json`; follow `.standards/` security, JSDoc, localization, Firebase, API, and unit-test guidance. No telemetry or new orchestration framework is introduced. Do not duplicate backend report calculations. Add automated cases for relevant invalid inputs, missing data, permissions, exports and cancellation. Keep examples synchronized with help and tests.

## Deployment and release checklist

- [ ] Verify Node/platform support, tests, coverage, lint, package contents, executable permissions and example commands using fixtures or an approved test identity.
- [ ] Check guide links, option defaults, date semantics, credential handling, output schemas, exit codes, and known limitations.
- [ ] Deploy `targetEventCapture`, `targetEventCleanup`, and the updated `sonaDashboard` API together through the reviewed release workflow. Match the capture region to the database location; default is us-central1 and the default project RTDB instance.
- [ ] In an isolated environment, create/update/hit/remove a synthetic target and verify delivery, retry/dedup, short-lived lifecycle, reconnect, source/snapshot handoff, gaps, access loss, close/rollover and listener cleanup. Do not send real notifications or modify production reports for a test.
- [ ] Establish live capture-lag evidence against the 60-second operational budget, confirm failed-trigger alerts, and measure expected connection/database load before claiming production latency or completeness.
- [ ] Verify same-project TOTP sign-in and refresh with an authorized account; never publish credential files or capture secrets in screenshots/logs.
- [ ] Record the version, new event interface/schema, replay limits and compatibility notes; advertise watch only after its backend is deployed and verified.

These deployment items are release gates, not claims of actions already performed. Source tests and fixture checks do not certify a live deployment. Rollback removes/disables the new public endpoint and capture/cleanup functions through reviewed deployment; it does not alter target/report source records. Retained journals can expire naturally. A CLI user can continue finite reporting against compatible existing APIs.

## Higher-tier CLI access and distribution

CLI 0.1.0 uses `/api/cli/product/*` and `/api/cli/access`. The original `/api/product/*` dashboard routes retain their existing report permissions. Clients cannot establish their identity by a User-Agent/header; the boundary is the separately authorized CLI service contract. Dashboard access may permit the same underlying data independently. This feature does not promise to prevent automation of a user's otherwise authorized dashboard reads.

The canonical permission is `cli.access`. New Desk Intelligence and Firm Wide Enterprise entitlement versions include it. Entity Core cannot acquire it through feature overrides. Custom licenses require an explicit grant through the existing governed entitlement workflow. Complimentary/internal billing does not bypass license or permission checks. Current membership, organization/subscription status, effective dates and per-report permissions still apply. Downgrades to Entity Core revoke CLI access even if an old entitlement snapshot retains the bit. Live reads repeat the check after waiting.

No automatic customer backfill is performed. Before release, inventory eligible organizations and reissue entitlement versions through the existing audited subscription-management workflow. Confirm the new permission in `/api/access/me`, grant only approved licenses, and record rollback to the previous entitlement version. Missing permission fails closed. Do not edit historical immutable entitlement snapshots in place.

`GET /api/cli/release` returns a versioned manifest; `GET /api/cli/download` returns the fixed archive after fresh authorization. Both responses are private/no-store. The bundled archive contains only npm's CLI file allowlist, its version and a SHA-256 checksum. Package possession is not authorization. No package registry or new paid hosting is required.

Customer guides are exported with `npm run docs:cli:sync` in the paired frontend checkout from these maintained Markdown files. Commit the generated snapshot with each contract change. Public routes are `/docs/cli` and `/docs/cli/:slug`; signed-in setup is `/dashboard/cli`. Public documentation contains no private environment, session or download credential. Recheck both source tests and customer flows after changing this contract.

# Postman collection

Import the [collection](sona-cli.postman_collection.json) and an empty [local environment](sona-cli.local.postman_environment.json) or [live environment](sona-cli.live.postman_environment.json) into Postman. The collection uses schema v2.1. It contains:

- **Authentication (live only):** password sign-in, enrolled authenticator challenge completion and token renewal against the fixed Google endpoints.
- **Product API:** account access, seven existing product data endpoints, initial live snapshot, cursor replay, reset/gap behavior, release manifest and authenticated archive (13 requests).
- **Negative cases:** missing authentication, missing MFA and missing entitlements on every product route; invalid selectors/cursors, history retention, expired and malformed sessions (35 requests).

The isolated acceptance run executes **48 product/access and negative requests** through the real Express app with actual Auth, Firestore and Realtime Database emulators. It does not execute the three real Google authentication requests. Emulator MFA claims are deliberately simulated and are not evidence of a real TOTP sign-in. Source-change events are synthetic inputs to the capture handler; deployed trigger activation remains a separate live check.

## Private environment configuration

Templates contain empty values only. Set values privately in the selected local environment. If your organization uses Postman Vault, resolve approved secrets privately for the request; this collection does not automatically read Vault entries. Never share/sync populated credentials, export a populated environment, commit tokens, or enable retention of secret run values. [Postman variable guidance](https://learning.postman.com/docs/use/send-requests/variables/variables) explains scope; masking alone does not make an exported secret safe.

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| baseUrl | Trusted service root, before `/api/cli/product`; loopback for isolated runs, HTTPS for approved live use. |
| organizationId | Optional licensed organization; empty selects the account default. |
| reportDate | Known completed and accessible daily report, YYYY-MM-DD. |
| year / week | ISO year/week of the selected saved weekly report. |
| month | Accessible calendar month, YYYY-MM. |
| liveDate | Current New York date. |
| replayCursor | A server-issued position within the retained journal for live replay; do not fabricate a claim of complete recovery. |
| outsideRetentionDate | A date outside the limited test identity's history window. |
| apiKey / email / password / totpCode | Private runtime inputs for approved real-account password/TOTP sign-in. |
| idToken / refreshToken | Current session values, set by successful live auth requests or supplied privately. |
| firstFactorIdToken | A valid first-factor-only test token, expected to fail MFA checks. |
| restrictedIdToken | Authorized test identity with no relevant product grants, expected to fail entitlement checks. |
| limitedIdToken | Authorized test identity with a limited history window. |
| expiredIdToken / invalidIdToken | Expired test token and deliberately malformed test value for failure checks. |
| mfaPendingCredential / mfaEnrollmentId / liveCursor | Values obtained during the run. Keep them private; do not export populated run state. |

## Running

For local acceptance, install the isolated tool package and use the emulator command documented in [development](../development.md). The harness creates synthetic users and records only in `demo-sona-cli`, supplies environment values in memory and executes the exact committed collection using Newman. No existing customer subscription, target/report history or notification is changed.

For the live phase, first obtain deployment approval and an authorized test account. Use the approved Postman application, configure private values, then run the authentication requests in order with a fresh authenticator code. Authentication scripts store returned values in the current environment; keep values local and clear them after use. The Google responses differ from the service's standard response envelope, so they have separate assertions.

Run **Product API** only after authenticating and selecting real report dates within your license. Run **Negative cases** only with the appropriate authorized test identities and explicit scenario inputs; they do not create or modify memberships. A missing test identity is a blocker, not a reason to mark a scenario passed. Collection requests are read-only apart from account sign-in/token renewal; there are no report-generation, customer-management, notification or target-write requests.

The automated collection asserts status, standard response envelope, safe failures and endpoint-specific shapes. The real-route CLI tests additionally reconcile daily/weekly/monthly fixture totals and exercise runtime permissions. An importable collection and a passing local run do not certify deployed endpoints or real MFA challenge completion.

The development-only Newman dependency tree has documented remaining upstream advisories. It is isolated from application dependencies and restricted to trusted fixture execution; see [tool restrictions](../../../tools/postman/README.md). Do not use that pinned test tool with real secrets or untrusted collections.

## Weekly stats

### Historical source audit and recovery

`scripts/captureReportHistory.js` captures explicit date-bounded monthly sources
with GET requests only and records SHA-256 hashes in a private local manifest.
`scripts/auditReportSources.js` verifies those hashes and audits the captured
history offline. Neither script writes Firebase or sends notifications.

`helpers/reportSourceRecovery.js` proposes a missing five-minute candle only
when all five unique one-minute records have valid OHLC and overlapping bars
from the same date match the existing five-minute feed exactly. Missing,
duplicate or inconsistent minutes remain unresolved. Source-feed conflicts and
missing target records prevent a date from entering the replay candidates.
Candidates must still pass the existing daily generator's validation.

`scripts/replayReportHistory.js` runs the existing daily and weekly generators
against the verified local capture, in date order, and recalculates monthly views.
It has no database write or delivery methods. Its review manifest includes each
proposed path, payload hash, original value and Firebase-normalized precondition
hash. Known unresolved saved sources receive proposed `sourceValidation: blocked`
metadata; the original statistics remain in the backup. Once applied, product
reads withhold those daily/weekly values and monthly calculations exclude them.
Successful daily regeneration replaces the blocked marker with validated source
metadata. No source-quality markers are applied by the offline replay itself.

`stats/nq/5m/weekly/2026/26` for the week whose Friday is 2026-06-26).

### How it's built

The generator accepts a strict Friday date and uses New York session boundaries.
It requires a daily report for every expected open session, including zero-target
days. The existing calendar rules and stored overrides identify closures and early
closes. Missing reports, unfinished weeks, mismatched daily totals, and invalid hit
times stop generation. Weekly and monthly share `validateSavedDailyReport` for
date/count consistency, duplicate targets, session clocks (including early
closes), and report finalization timestamps. Weekly additionally requires usable
resolution times for every hit; monthly retains missing-measurement sample counts.
Legacy zero-target accuracy is normalized in memory only. Zero-target sessions
count toward coverage but are N/A in daily accuracy history and excluded from the
unweighted daily-average accuracy; a day with targets and no hits still contributes
0%. This checks daily-report consistency; it does not rerun the
daily market-data validation or repair historical source gaps.

Generation reads the calendar without syncing it and shares monthly snapshots
between the selected week and its comparison windows. The scheduler waits for
saving and delivery and propagates failures. Week-year keys follow ISO weeks,
including week 53 and Mondays that fall in the preceding calendar year.

Daily and weekly comparison windows also validate saved dates, totals, session
clocks and gaps between expected sessions. An invalid window is omitted as a
whole, rather than silently dropping bad days and inflating the comparison.
Daily generation uses bounded calendar reads too, so daily repair dry runs do
not trigger calendar synchronization. Repair dates are validated and processed
in chronological order; a conflicting runtime project stops the operation.

The existing `regenWeeklyDoc.js` tool requires an explicit project and Friday dates.
It defaults to a dry run. Writing requires both `--write` and a matching
`--confirm-project`; regeneration sends no notifications. The tool uses runtime
credentials rather than a hardcoded legacy service-account file.

## Bucket stats ("Hit Rate by Target Type")

Owner file: [functions/helpers/bucketStats.js](../functions/helpers/bucketStats.js)

**What a "bucket" is.** A bucket is a group of past targets that share the same
characteristics — **direction** (bullish/bearish) and **time of day**
(morning 9:30–11:30, midday 11:30–14:00, afternoon 14:00–16:00). It is exactly
what the UI labels a **"Target Type"** (e.g. "Bullish · Morning"). The word
"bucket" is internal only; it never appears in the product or the API.

**Why it exists.** A single global average ("SONA hits ~85%") is generic. Bucket
stats let a new target be matched to *its own kind* so the live alert can say
"targets like this hit X%; when they hit, price typically retraces ~Y pts first."

**What each bucket holds** (computed over a recent rolling window, ~20 sessions):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n`, `hits` | targets in the bucket, and how many hit |
| `hitRate` | hits / n, as a percent |
| `medianTimeMin` | median minutes-to-hit (hits only) |
| `meanTimeMin` | mean minutes-to-hit — the "real average" with slow outliers counted in full (hits only) |
| `p90TimeMin` | 90th-percentile time-to-hit — the slow tail (hits only) |
| `maxTimeMin` | slowest hit observed in the window (hits only) |
| `pctWithin5Min` | share of hits that resolved within 5 minutes |
| `medianDrift`, `p25Drift`, `p75Drift`, `maxDrift` | retraction median, middle-50% band, deepest (hits only) |
| `meanDrift`, `p90Drift` | mean retraction (real average — deep outliers included) and 90th-percentile (deep tail) (hits only) |
| `pctWithin10` | share of hits that retraced ≤10 pts |

Three levels are always produced so a lookup can fall back when a narrow bucket
is too thin: `"bullish|morning"` → `"bullish"` → `"all"`. `resolveBucket()`
walks that ladder, using a bucket only if it meets the minimum sample
(`minSample`, default 15), otherwise dropping to the broader level.

Retraction and time are **only measured on hits** — a miss never reverses, so
it has no retraction to measure.

**Why mean + p90 + max in addition to median.** Median is the typical case,
but it hides the tail. When a user looks at a target that's been open 18
minutes against a 5-min median, the median alone reads "this is broken." Mean,
p90, and max add the missing context: *yes, the typical is 5 min, but the real
average is 14 (a few slow ones), p90 is 38, and the slowest in 20 sessions was
84.* The full distribution is honest about outliers without throwing them out.

**Where it lives:**

- Embedded on the weekly doc (`bucketStats`) for the Weekly page grid + the
  retraction-depth curve (`bucketStats.retractionCurve`).
- Embedded on the **daily doc** (`rawPayload.bucketStats`) so the Daily
  Performance page shows a baseline that matches the date being viewed — not
  just today's live snapshot. Generated lazily by the daily run (commit
  `6236a69`) and fail-soft (a missing block never blocks the report).
- Published once per day to `stats/nq/5m/buckets/current` (a stable snapshot) by
  the end-of-day daily run, so the live Today's Targets page and the
  alert-stamping path read one fresh copy. Repopulate on demand with
  `node scripts/regenBucketsSnapshot.js`. The same write also co-publishes
  `lateResolvers` (see below).

## Late resolver stats ("when a target runs past 5 min")

Owner file: [functions/helpers/lateResolverStats.js](../functions/helpers/lateResolverStats.js)

**What it is.** A separate cohort that filters down to targets that took
longer than a threshold (default **5 minutes**) — or never resolved at all —
across the same rolling 20-session window used by bucket stats. It answers the
question the Open Target card needs at minute 6 onward: *"when one of mine is
past 5 min, what usually happens?"*

**Why it exists.** Comparing a 52-minute open target against the all-targets
5-minute median is misleading — half of *all* targets resolve in 5 min, but
once you're past that, you're no longer in the typical cohort. The late-resolver
block re-baselines against the right peer group.

**What each group holds** (same `direction|session` → `direction` → `all`
ladder as bucket stats, with `minSample=8`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | late targets in this group (hit-late + never-resolved) |
| `hits` | how many of those eventually hit |
| `eventualHitRate` | hits / n, as a percent |
| `neverResolved` | count that ran past the threshold and never hit |
| `medianTimeMin`, `meanTimeMin`, `p90TimeMin`, `maxTimeMin` | how long the eventual-hits took |
| `medianRetraction`, `meanRetraction`, `p25Retraction`, `p75Retraction`, `p90Retraction`, `maxRetraction` | retraction distribution on the eventual-hits |

The block at the top of the payload also carries `windowSessions`,
`thresholdMin` (the late cutoff, default 5), `totalTargets`, `totalLate`,
`share` (totalLate / totalTargets %), and `minSample`.

**Where it lives:**

- Embedded on the daily doc as `rawPayload.lateResolverStats` so the Daily
  Performance "Late Resolvers (>5 min)" KPI tile shows a baseline aligned to
  the date being viewed.
- Co-published with the bucket snapshot to
  `stats/nq/5m/buckets/current/lateResolvers` so the alert-stamping path can
  read one fresh copy without a second query.

### `lateContext` on a target

Whenever an alert fires, `getTargetLateContext` resolves the live snapshot's
late-cohort group for that target's direction × session and stamps the
display-ready block on the target as `rawPayload.lateContext`. This is what
the Open Target card reads to flip its baseline once a target crosses the
threshold. Stamped fields mirror the group fields above plus `direction`,
`session`, `matched` (the bucket key that won the fallback ladder), `level`
(`direction+session` / `direction` / `all`), `fellBack` (true when the narrow
group was too thin), `thresholdMin`, and `throughDate`.

`lateContext` is **null** when the live snapshot has no late-cohort data yet
(insufficient history) or the helper isn't deployed. The Open Target card
treats `null` as "stay on the normal baseline" and falls back silently.

## Generation flow (daily)

1. Read `targets/nq/5m/{YYYY-MM}/{DD}` — list of alerts that day.
2. Read or fetch the day's 5m chart (Firebase first, FMP as fallback).
3. For each target:
   - **Pre-written branch** — `target.targetReached === true` already?
     Trust the live 1m hit data. Preserve `targetReachedTimeframe`
     (default `"1m"`).
   - **5m fallback branch** — walk subsequent 5m candles until one
     crosses the target. Stamp `targetReachedTimeframe = "5m"`.
4. Compute retraction (1m precise if available, 5m fallback otherwise).
5. Build aggregates (`targetStats`).
6. Pass to transformer → enterprise payload (medians, miss analysis,
   temporal patterns, price distribution).
7. Distribute to Discord/webhook/email and write the stats doc to RTDB.

| **Retraction** / "drift away from the target" | "Heat", "drawdown" |
| **Hit** / "reversed back to the target" | "Filled", "took profit" |
| **Nullified** (price shot through the target before reversing) | "Stopped out" |

`entryPrice` and `entryHeatPoints` are stored in the per-target record but
are **internal diagnostics only** — never surface them in tiles, tables,
captions, or charts.

### Tile layout (top of page)

Driven entirely by the raw daily payload + `engulfingCandleList`:

| Tile | Source | Caption |
|---|---|---|
| Streak | `consecutiveStreak.longest` | "longest run of hit targets today" |
| First target | `firstTargetHit` | "Hit" / "Missed" badge |
| Typical hit time | `resolutionTimes.median` | "fastest N · slowest N" |
| Average retraction | `avgRetraction` | "how far price typically drifted away from the target before reversing back" |
| Tightness | `pctHitWithin10pts` | "share of hit targets that stayed within 10 pts before reversing" |
| Biggest retraction | `maxRetraction` | "the deepest drift that still reversed back to hit" |
| Late Resolvers (>5 min) | `lateResolverStats.groups.all` | "when a target runs past 5 min: eventual hit rate, median/mean/p90 time, never resolved" |

Each time-or-retraction tile also carries a sub-line `"20-session: median X · mean Y · p90 Z"` pulled from `trailingStats.pooled` so the headline number is read against the full 20-session distribution — not just an average of daily medians.

### Per-target row

Show the target, the retraction, and the hit. Suggested copy:

```
▼  9:30 AM  Bearish target 29,633.25
   Drifted 215 pts away (worst price 29,848.25) before reversing
   ✅ Hit at 10:00 AM · 30 min
```

```
▼  2:00 PM  Bearish target 28,784.75
   ❌ Did not reverse — closest approach 28,818.75 (34 pts short)
```

Color the retraction line by drift size:
- ≤ 10 pts → green ("tight")
- 11–50 pts → neutral
- 51–100 pts → amber
- 100+ pts → red ("deep retraction")

### Forward-looking note

`avgRetraction` is the metric that will eventually drive a "where to wait
for the reversal" prediction — that's why we measure it per target and
surface the average prominently. Treat it as the headline stat alongside
accuracy.

## Calendar-month History reports

The dashboard's History page now offers a **Calendar month** view alongside
its existing rolling views. The authenticated `GET /api/product/monthly?month=YYYY-MM`
endpoint requires the History entitlement and applies the organization's history
retention before reading any daily reports. A selected month must fit entirely
within retention. An inaccessible prior month is omitted without failing the
selected month.

Monthly reports are calculated on read, from saved daily target rows. There is
no monthly document write, schedule, delivery, notification, or historical
backfill in this change. Once an approved daily correction is saved, the monthly
view reflects it on its next request; saved weekly reports still need their
existing regeneration workflow.

### Definitions and coverage

- New York calendar months and the existing reporting-session/holiday rules
  define the period. Today's report is excluded until its session closes.
  A saved calculation timestamp before session close is also rejected.
- Accuracy is total hits divided by total targets; timing and pullback
  distributions pool individual measured hits. They are not averages of daily
  or weekly percentages or medians. Display rounding happens after pooling.
- Zero-target sessions are included in session counts and volume-per-session
  denominators; accuracy is N/A. Historical zero-target `NaN%` display values are
  normalized in memory only. Closed dates remain in coverage metadata and are
  omitted from the daily table. Missing, pending and inconsistent weekday
  reports remain visible.
- Dates with mismatched totals, duplicate targets or known invalid clocks are
  flagged and excluded. Coverage remains incomplete. Target streaks stop at
  missing/inconsistent dates; zero-target and closed days do not add losses.
- Timing, pullback, miss-distance and target-distance sample sizes are explicit.
  Missing measurements do not become zero. Best/worst days include target counts.
- Slow hits mean more than five minutes but still hit by that session's close.
  Cross-session fills are not evaluated by this view and never change daily
  outcomes or monthly hit rate.
- Comparisons use the prior calendar month only, and are hidden if it is
  incomplete. Partial-month volumes are compared as targets/hits per included
  session. Rates and medians retain the same definitions on both sides.
- Coverage validates saved report consistency, not underlying candle-history
  completeness. Older calculation versions are labeled for review. The separate
  source audit and offline replay propose source repairs; the monthly view does
  not repair missing price history itself.

### Reuse and request cost

The daily generator's pure calculators now live in `helpers/targetReportStats.js`;
its existing exports remain compatible. Calendar reads are shared with weekly
reporting through `helpers/reportCalendar.js`. Monthly calculations reuse those
helpers plus the existing direction/session and slow-hit calculators.

A request performs one bounded calendar read and at most two bounded daily-month
snapshot reads, shared across all displayed statistics. The prior comparison
returns summaries instead of a second target dataset. The selected month returns
compact target fields without full source candle histories. The dashboard loads
only its selected rolling/monthly view and ignores obsolete monthly responses,
including retries and switching away from and back to the same month.

The monthly view includes daily accuracy and stacked hit/miss volume graphs,
plus timing and pullback distributions. Daily charts omit closed and unfinished
sessions, preserve missing reports as gaps, and show zero-target accuracy as
unavailable. Distribution counts include only measured hits and display their
sample sizes. Charts use the dashboard's existing ApexCharts components.

### Historical replay verification — October 22, 2026

The captured November 2024–October 2026 history produced 440 proposed daily
reports (December 24, 2024–October 22, 2026), 68 complete weekly reports and 60
recoverable five-minute candles. Headline values change on 116 daily reports.
The independent verifier checked all 645 proposed paths and all 24 monthly
views. Eight historical months have complete validated coverage after replay.

The proposal also marks 48 saved daily and 29 saved weekly reports as blocked
because their sources cannot yet be verified. This preserves the stored report
and adds quality metadata; product reads withhold its statistics. Closed-session
reports containing targets are included in these holds until calendar/source
conflicts are resolved. These counts describe local proposals, not applied writes.

`scripts/verifyReportReplay.js` checks payload and backup hashes, daily source
validation, independently derived hit counts and durations, weekly reconciliation
to daily target rows, and monthly reconciliation to included days and targets.
Backups use Firebase's empty-value and array/object representation semantics for
stable before/after hashes. The offline adapter cannot write to Firebase or send
report notifications.

### Release preparation and remaining gate — October 22, 2026

Phases 1–3 are committed: backend `e8bffa5`, `c14e53a`, `2a05635`;
dashboard `4cf5919`, `3046e8a`. Phase 4 adds the final read-only preflight,
release evidence, and an email-delivery fix that preserves an explicitly
unavailable comparison instead of replacing it with the legacy fallback.

- The complete backend suite passes 1,058 tests; the dashboard suite passes
  531 tests. Backend lint and dashboard production build pass. Two existing
  customer-admin hook warnings remain. The production entry bundle is
  341.55 KiB gzip against a 400 KiB budget.
- A fresh bounded capture matched all 100 source snapshots. All 645 proposal
  before-values match those sources. `scripts/preflightReportReplay.js` rejects
  changed sources, mismatched project/range, unrelated paths and overlapping
  writes. Run it again immediately before release; this check is not a lock.
- The updated Firebase preview uses proposed October data through October 22.
  Four charts, closed-date row removal, missing weekdays and mobile layout were
  checked. It is a frozen preview, not a live dashboard deployment.
- The source archive currently deployed for `sonaDashboard` was compared to
  the working tree: changed runtime files are confined to reporting and its
  shared helpers. The release targets are `ecTargetStatsOnDemand`,
  `ecTargetStatsScheduled`, `ecTargetStatsWeekly`,
  `ecTargetsStatsScheduledWeekly`, and `sonaDashboard`, plus dashboard hosting.
- Production dependency audits remain unresolved: backend has 9 moderate and
  no high/critical findings; dashboard has 123 findings including 50 high and
  8 critical. Dashboard counts include build tooling declared as production
  dependencies, but browser-used packages also have advisories. This reporting
  verification is not a clean security audit; no unrelated upgrades were made.

The final release decision must acknowledge that 48 daily reports and 29 weekly
reports will be withheld until source issues are resolved. Daily corrections
span December 24, 2024–October 22, 2026; quality holds extend to December 2, 2024.
The 68 complete weekly replacements end between January 3, 2025 and August 14,
2026. Later completed weeks remain incomplete; the current week is unfinished.

After that release approval: recheck sources, deploy reporting code/dashboard,
apply the reviewed source repairs and quality holds, save daily corrections in
date order, then refresh complete weeks. Use conditional before-value checks
for every write and read each result back. Do not replay notifications. Monthly
views refresh on read. Preserve the existing before-value backups; rollback
must restore only records still matching this release's after-values, in reverse
dependency order. Verify the next daily and weekly scheduled runs separately.

No historical writes or live function/dashboard deployment were performed in
these preparation phases. The only hosting deployment was the preview channel.

title: Time to Resolution
markdown:
# Time to Resolution

"Time to Resolution" (TtR) is how long a target took to get hit, measured
from the **close** of the alert candle to the **close** of the hit bar.

> History note (2026-06 clock fix): `targetReachedDuration` strings written
> before the fix measured open-to-open, which silently added the alert
> candle's own minutes to every duration (~4 min inflation vs this
> definition). The live writer, the EOD generator, and the enterprise
> temporal patterns now all measure close-to-close. The EOD generator
> recomputes durations from timestamps, so re-running
> `scripts/regenStatsDoc.js <date>` heals old stats docs; the raw target
> records keep their original strings until backfilled.

## The precision problem

We have two data sources at EOD:

- **5m chart** — always present.
- **1m history** — present only from **2026-06-09 onward** (and only on days
  where `chartHistory1m` ran). Before that date there is no 1m data at all.

If a hit was detected live by `chartHistory1m`, we know the exact 1m bar
that took the target out — TtR is precise to the minute. If we only have
the 5m chart, we know the 5m bar that crossed but we don't know which of
the five minutes inside it was the trigger.

The system has to do **one thing on days with 1m data and a different
thing on days without it**. Both modes share the same fields; the
difference is encoded in a single tag.

## The `targetReachedTimeframe` tag

Every "hit" write stamps `targetReachedTimeframe` on the target record:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"1m"` | Hit was detected on a 1m bar — TtR is exact (per-minute). |
| `"5m"` | Hit was detected on a 5m bar — TtR is bracketed by a 5-minute window. |

The tag flows from the target record → `engulfingCandleList` rows in the
stats doc → `targetLog` rows in the enterprise transform → frontend.

## Where each path stamps the tag

| Path | File | Stamps |
|---|---|---|
| Live 1m hit detector | [functions/features/ecTargets/daily/ecTargets_targetHit.js](../functions/features/ecTargets/daily/ecTargets_targetHit.js) | `"1m"` |
| Backfill script | [functions/scripts/backfillHitTimes.js](../functions/scripts/backfillHitTimes.js) | `"1m"` (only runs when 1m history exists) |
| EOD daily stats — pre-written branch | [functions/features/ecTargetStats/daily/ecTargetsStats_generate_daily_enterprise_v0.js](../functions/features/ecTargetStats/daily/ecTargetsStats_generate_daily_enterprise_v0.js), [..._v3.js](../functions/features/ecTargetStats/daily/ecTargetsStats_generate_daily_v3.js) | preserves `currentCandle.targetReachedTimeframe \|\| "1m"` |
| EOD daily stats — 5m fallback branch | same files | `"5m"` |

## Close-time math

The helper that converts an open-time stamp to a close-time stamp lives in
[functions/helpers/closeTime.js](../functions/helpers/closeTime.js):

```js
const computeReachedCloseTimestamp = (targetReachedTime, timeframe) => {
  const minutes = getTimeframeMinutes(timeframe) || 1;
  return String(parseInt(targetReachedTime, 10) + minutes * 60);
};
```

`resolveReachedCloseTimestamp(target)` reads the stored
`target.targetReachedTimeframe` (defaulting to `"1m"`) and adds the right
number of seconds. **Never hardcode `+60s` here** — pre-2026-06-09 records
were 5m-detected and adding only 60 seconds gave a misleading "1 min" TtR.

## What the frontend should show

- **`targetReachedTimeframe === "1m"`** → render TtR exactly. Times resolve
  to the minute (e.g. `9:43 AM`, `10:09 AM`).
- **`targetReachedTimeframe === "5m"`** → render TtR as the 5m window
  (`9:35 AM`–`9:40 AM` close), and consider showing an "Est." badge or
  similar so users don't mistake a 5-minute estimate for a 1-minute reading.
- **Missing tag** → legacy record. Treat as `"1m"` (live hit path always
  wrote 1m precision), unless the day predates 1m capture, in which case
  re-run the EOD job (which will fall back to 5m and stamp the tag).

## Backfilling old records

`functions/scripts/regenStatsDoc.js` regenerates the stats doc for any date
without firing Discord/email/webhook side effects. Use it when:

- The 5m fallback writer changed (re-stamp the tag everywhere).
- The retraction formula changed (re-compute the away-from-target drift).
- A live hit was missed (the 5m fallback will catch it at EOD).

```bash
cd functions
node scripts/regenStatsDoc.js 2026-06-08
```

## Quick sanity check

A row tagged `"1m"` whose `targetReachedTime` is **on** a 5m boundary
(e.g. `:00`, `:05`, `:10`) is suspicious — it might be a 5m-fallback row
that was tagged incorrectly or a coincidence. A row tagged `"1m"` whose
time is off-grid (e.g. `:43`) is definitely a real 1m hit.

title: Retraction Logic
markdown:
# Retraction Logic

## The trader's-eye picture

HVI prints a **target** — the top of a 5m bullish candle, or the bottom
of a 5m bearish candle. After it prints, one of two things happens:

1. Price **shoots through** the target — the target nullifies; nothing to
   measure.
2. Price **drifts away from** the target first, then **reverses back** and
   hits it. That away-leg is the **retraction**.

We measure retraction because it tells us how far price typically wanders
from a target before turning around to hit it. Once we have a stable
average, we can predict where to wait for the reversal — that's the
forward-looking goal of this metric.

> Plain definition: *retraction is how far price drifted away from the
> target during the away-and-back move that eventually resolved it.*

## Direction-aware

The baseline is the **target price** (the top of a bullish alert candle,
the bottom of a bearish one — stamped on the record as `targetPrice`):

- **Bullish target** (price needs to rise to `targetPrice`): retraction is
  measured downward from the target price. Worst price = lowest low seen
  during the drift.
- **Bearish target** (price needs to fall to `targetPrice`): retraction is
  measured upward from the target price. Worst price = highest high seen
  during the drift.

```js
retractionPoints = isBullish
  ? targetPrice - worstLow
  : worstHigh - targetPrice;
```

If price never drifted away from the target, retraction is `0` (clamped).

## Internal-only companion fields: `entryPrice` / `entryHeatPoints`

The record also stores two diagnostic fields that share the retraction
window but use a different baseline:

| Field | Baseline | What it's for |
|---|---|---|
| `retractionPoints` | `targetPrice` | **The user-facing metric.** Drift from target during the away-and-back leg. |
| `entryHeatPoints` | price at alert close (`entryPrice`) | Internal diagnostic — strips the alert candle's own height out of the drift number for engineering scans. |

These exist because on a **wide alert candle** (e.g. a violent cash open
spanning 150+ points), the candle closes far from its own extreme — so
`retractionPoints` can read large even though price marched cleanly toward
the target after the close. `entryHeatPoints` lets a developer see "did
the drift happen during the alert candle, or after it?".

> **Do not surface `entryPrice` or `entryHeatPoints` in user-facing UI or
> reports.** They are storage-only fields for diagnostics. The Daily
> Performance page, Discord embeds, and emails all speak in terms of
> retraction (drift from the target).

Baseline source: **1m path** — open of the first 1m bar after the alert
candle closes. **5m path** — the alert candle's own close (fallback: first
post-close bar's open). Both clamp at `0`.

## The formula (current)

Owner: [functions/features/ecTargets/daily/ecTargets_targetHit.js](../functions/features/ecTargets/daily/ecTargets_targetHit.js)
→ `computeRetraction`. The window is `[alertClose, hitBarClose]` on 1m bars.

For each 1m bar in the window we use:

- **All bars before the hit bar** — full `high` and `low`.
- **The hit bar itself** — `open` only (we ignore its full high/low).

Why? The hit bar is the candle that crossed the target. Its high/low spans
the move *through* the target, which is no longer "retraction" — it's the
move that resolved the target. Using only the hit bar's open captures
"where price was sitting when the bar that took us out began", which is
the last honest measurement of the pre-hit drift away from the target.

```js
// Bullish
const worstLow = Math.min(
  ...preHitBars.map((b) => parseFloat(b.low)),
  parseFloat(hitBar.open),
);
retractionPoints = targetPrice - worstLow;

// Bearish
const worstHigh = Math.max(
  ...preHitBars.map((b) => parseFloat(b.high)),
  parseFloat(hitBar.open),
);
retractionPoints = worstHigh - targetPrice;
```

If the hit bar has no stored `open`, the calculation returns null rather
than guess (the EOD job may then fill it via the 5m fallback below).

## Why we care about the hit-bar-open

A real example from 2026-06-10 — alert `mq8426jh` (28778 bearish target):

- Cash open at 9:30 had a violent volatile candle.
- The 9:35 EST 1m bar ranged from ~28950 down to 28778 — **the same bar
  that took out the target also printed the day's high**.
- Naive formula (full high/low of every bar in window) reported
  retraction = 123 points.
- Corrected formula (pre-hit-bars-full + hit-bar-open-only) reports
  retraction = 3 points.

The 123 points is real price action, but it happened *during* the move
that hit the target, not before it. The 3-point reading correctly says
"price was 3 points away from the target when the resolution candle began
— the drift was effectively zero".

## Precision modes

| `retractionPrecision` | Source | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `"1m"` | computed from `history/nq/1m/...` | Per-minute resolution; trustable for tight retractions. |
| `"5m"` | computed from the day's 5m chart | Coarser; only set on days with no 1m history. |
| `null` | none | History was missing on both timeframes. |

The 5m path lives in `computeRetractionFrom5m` inside
[functions/features/ecTargetStats/daily/ecTargetsStats_generate_daily_v3.js](../functions/features/ecTargetStats/daily/ecTargetsStats_generate_daily_v3.js).
It applies the same rule on 5m bars:

- Window starts at the **alert candle close** (the alert candle's own
  range never counts — the target didn't exist yet).
- 5m bars that closed before the hit contribute full high/low.
- The 5m bar **containing** the hit contributes only its open. (A live 1m
  hit timestamp can fall mid-bar; the containing bar is still treated as
  the hit bar.)
- No stored open on the hit bar → null fields.

> History note: before 2026-06 (Phase 3 fix) this fallback used the full
> high/low of every window bar **including** the alert and hit candles, so
> `retractionPrecision: "5m"` values written before then read larger than
> they should. Re-run `regenStatsDoc.js` on affected dates to correct them.

## Storage

Written alongside the hit fields on the target record:

```
targets/nq/5m/{YYYY-MM}/{DD}/{pushId}/
  retractionPoints       — number (e.g. 4.75) — drift from target, user-facing
  retractionWorstPrice   — string (e.g. "28781.00") — worst price during the drift
  retractionPrecision    — "1m" | "5m" | null
  entryHeatPoints        — number — internal diagnostic only (see above)
  entryPrice             — string — internal diagnostic only (see above)
```

## Backfilling

`functions/scripts/backfillHitTimes.js` replays target records against 1m
history. If a record's stored `retractionPoints` differs from the
recomputed value, the script writes a retraction-only update (preserving
the original hit time) so previously-mismeasured retractions get corrected
without changing TtR.

```bash
cd functions
node scripts/backfillHitTimes.js 2026-06-10
```

## Diagnostic helpers

Read-only utilities to investigate a suspect retraction:

- `scripts/inspectRetraction.js` — dumps every 1m bar in the retraction
  window for a given alert.
- `scripts/scanRetractionOutliers.js` — sorts all stored retractions for a
  date so outliers stand out.
- `scripts/checkOpenCoverage.js` — verifies that every 1m bar has an
  `open` field (older bars sometimes don't).
